commands.desc: Asks Rancher to upgrade the Helm release <release> in --namespace on --cluster through the upgrade action of a ClusterRepo: Rancher fetches the chart version and runs Helm in a pod. A newer version, an older version (a downgrade) and a change of values are all upgrades; Rancher has no rollback action. The server has no dry-run for this action; the preview comes from server reads (previewSource serverReads): the App (it must exist, with the status deployed, failed or superseded), the ClusterRepo (it must be enabled), the chart and version in the index Rancher serves for the cluster, the chart's default values and annotations, the Helm release Secret the App's owner reference names (it holds the release's values), and the operations of the namespace (none may still be running for the release). It carries no resourceVersion precondition: --apply reads the App, the operations and the index entry again before it sends the request, and without --wait nothing checks for a change after that. The chart is the App's chart; --chart is accepted only with that name, and another chart is refused: install it as a new release with `rancher app install`. --repo defaults to the ClusterRepo named in the App's catalog.cattle.io/ui-source-repo annotation, and --version to the App's installed version. The upgrade accepts the installed version when the index Rancher serves for the cluster no longer lists it and the ClusterRepo is the one the App came from. The preview and the result then warn that its chart content is not compared between the preview and the request. An older --version than the installed version is a downgrade, which the preview names. Values: the release's values are the values the App's revision was installed or upgraded with. The command reads them from the release Secret through the Steve API with includeHelmData=true. It merges each --values file over them in order (- reads stdin once; null removes a key) and sends the result. That read needs permission to get Secrets in the release's namespace. Without it the command stops and names --reset-values. --reset-values sends only the --values files and the values rancher-cli adds, and Helm takes every other value from the chart's defaults. rancher-cli never asks Helm to reuse the release's values. After a failed upgrade the release's values are the values that failed, and the preview warns. The preview lists the path of every value that is added, removed or changed, never the values, except the values rancher-cli adds and the registry host, and counts the release's values that it sends unchanged. As the Rancher UI does, rancher-cli adds the cluster values and the registry values the release's values lack; --system-default-registry <host> sets both registry values over the release's values, and --no-system-default-registry sends neither. The Rancher UI sends only the difference from the chart's defaults; rancher-cli sends the release's values in full. Helm treats both requests the same, and the values Helm keeps with the next revision then differ from the ones the Rancher UI would keep. Refused: an App with the status uninstalled, uninstalling, pending-install, pending-upgrade, pending-rollback or unknown, an operation still running for the release, a chart that names another chart to install first (catalog.cattle.io/auto-install or auto-install-gvr), a version whose catalog.cattle.io/namespace or release-name annotation does not match the release (the installed version is exempt), a requires-gvr or permits-os annotation the target does not meet, --force with --take-ownership, and a request that changes nothing. These flags make no change: --wait, --timeout, --cluster, --namespace, --dry-run, --apply and --yes. --version and --repo make a change when they differ from the App, and --values when the merge changes a value. Every other flag makes a change. --helm-wait (default true; --helm-wait=false sends false) makes Helm wait for the chart's resources; --helm-timeout (default 10m, at least 1s, at most 15m) is Helm's timeout; the chart's hooks can make a run longer, and Rancher removes a run's access one hour after the operation starts. --history-max (1 to 100; Rancher uses 5 when it is omitted) is the maximum number of revisions Helm keeps for the release; Helm deletes the oldest before the run, never the last deployed one. Helm does not roll back a failed upgrade: the resources it already changed stay changed, and --cleanup-on-fail deletes only the resources the upgrade created. Without --wait the command returns once Rancher accepts the request, with the operation and the commands that follow it. With --wait (or --timeout, default 55m, at most 55m) it returns when Helm's run has finished: with the release's revision and status, or with Helm's error, the release's state and the command to run next.
examples: rancher app upgrade my-nginx --cluster prod --namespace web --values change.yaml --dry-run
rancher app upgrade my-nginx --cluster prod --namespace web --version 1.2.3 --apply --yes

commands.desc: One document answering what state a cluster is in, what it is made of, and how nodes join it: the management.cattle.io Cluster's id, name, state, and kubernetesVersion (the observed version first, then the provisioning spec's desired version for pending clusters, empty when neither exists), its agent connectivity (agent.connected and agent.ready from the management.cattle.io Cluster's Connected and Ready conditions with the failing condition's message, preferring Connected's; the section is present only when those conditions report an explicit True or False (a condition with status Unknown is ignored and never shows the agent as not connected) and each field only when its own condition does; an agent that is not connected or a False Ready condition adds a warning - the status of the provisioning.cattle.io Cluster cannot show an agent outage), the provisioning.cattle.io Cluster's ready flag (derived from the Ready condition when present; falls back to status.ready) and conditions, its machine pools (name, machineConfigRef, quantity, roles), its members (ClusterRoleTemplateBindings with display names resolved from Users and UserAttributes, each row reporting principal, displayName, role, binding (the name of the ClusterRoleTemplateBinding), and system; a failed binding read leaves the members field out of the JSON while the text output shows members: unavailable, with a warning naming the cause; a failure to look up display names leaves out only the display names, never rows; entries whose principal id starts with system: (Rancher's system principals, e.g. system://provisioning/...) carry system: true (accounts Rancher uses internally, not bindings an administrator added)), its machines (CAPI Machine objects in fleet-default filtered by the cluster.x-k8s.io/cluster-name label; each entry reports name, phase, and the first failing condition message - preferring conditions whose reason contains "Error"; a failed list leaves the machines field out of the JSON while the text output shows machines: unavailable, with a warning naming the cause; left out when the provisioning cluster was not found), and the commands in the default cluster registration token: nodeCommand and insecureNodeCommand (to add nodes), command and insecureCommand (to import a cluster), and manifestUrl. On an imported cluster (provisioning spec.rkeConfig absent), notApplicable lists the node command fields that are present but do not apply; such fields are marked, never left out. By default the registration section has only a message and a hint, and the commands are left out, because they contain the cluster registration token (a credential that lets anyone add nodes to the cluster); pass --registration to fetch and show them. With --registration, the node command options (--etcd, --controlplane, --worker, --node-name, --address, --internal-address, --label, --taint, --windows) compose the node commands as the Rancher UI does: registration.withOptions has nodeCommand and insecureNodeCommand: Rancher's node command, then the options in the Rancher UI's order, with each value in single quotes and all three roles when no role flag is given. The options apply only to a custom cluster (spec.rkeConfig set and no machine pools); on any other cluster, and without --registration, they are refused. Each value is checked before any request. A value is refused and never changed when it has a character the Rancher UI would remove, or when it breaks the Kubernetes rule for a label or taint key or value, or for a node name; a label key Rancher sets on the node itself is refused too. With any node command option, a failed registration token read fails the command. --windows composes windowsNodeCommand and insecureWindowsNodeCommand instead (-Address, -InternalAddress, -NodeName, and one -Taint; no role flag and no --label: the Windows node command already ends in -Worker and passes -Label), only where the Rancher UI shows the Windows node command for the server's Rancher version: the cluster is not K3s, runs Kubernetes v1.21.0 or newer, has calico or no CNI set (flannel too from Kubernetes v1.29.2 on Rancher v2.14 and newer), is connected and has etcd, control plane and worker nodes. A Kubernetes version that is not MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, a pre-release included, is refused too. A cluster that is not ready yet gives a retryable error. Each section can be missing without affecting the others: provisioningNote marks a confirmed missing provisioning Cluster; an unavailable or ambiguous lookup and a failed registration read leave out their sections with a warning naming the cause. If you cannot read part of the data, the command still exits 0: each section it could not read in full is named in data.degraded ({section, state, code, target}), and each entry has one warning. Finding the cluster by id or name and reading its management.cattle.io Cluster are required: the command fails when any of them fails. Sections that can degrade: provisioning (unavailable - the lookup of the provisioning.cattle.io Cluster that matches this cluster, one entry covering the status, machinePools, and machines, which are then left out), machines (unavailable - a machine list that failed after that Cluster was found), members (unavailable - the binding list; a failure to look up display names stays a warning), registration (unavailable - reading the cluster registration token).

commands.desc: Prints a kubeconfig whose user entry runs the rancher exec-credential plugin. One context reaches the cluster through the Rancher proxy. It also says whether this build sends the events that later recorded runs store in this config directory (sendsEvents in -o json): a release build sends none, and a development build sends only with an upload endpoint and recording on; with no endpoint, the text has a sending: none line that gives the reason. In a development build with RANCHER_CLI_EXPERIMENT set, it also lists the active experiments and the upload endpoint. A development build with the telemetryupload experiment sends the stored events of finished hours to that endpoint at most once an hour, after a recorded run, never from the kubectl exec plugin; with an endpoint, status shows the last upload attempt, the next attempt, the events waiting, the events of the current hour, and a warning for an upload lock that cannot be read. Creates nothing and works while recording is off.

commands.desc: Development builds with the telemetryupload experiment only. Records its attempt: the next automatic attempt comes about an hour later. Takes at most 30 seconds. Never runs from the kubectl exec plugin, and a release build refuses it. Its own run records no event. Exits 0 whatever the endpoint answered. sent counts every event in a request the endpoint answered with a 2xx, including the ones it refused; refused says how many. commands.desc: Groups results by --by (namespace|project|node|pod). --namespace, --project, and --node are filters that narrow every grouping: --node keeps only pods scheduled on that node; --namespace with --project requires one of the project's namespaces. --by node accepts only --node; combining --by node with --namespace or --project is a validation error. --project without --by returns one row for each of the project's namespaces (namespace grouping filtered to the project). --by project --project X returns a single row for that project. If no pods match --namespace or --node, the command reads the namespace or node you named: a missing one is NOT_FOUND, and one you are not allowed to read adds a warning to the result (with --project, a namespace outside the project is a validation error; --by node --node reads the node first, and an unreadable node there is an error; --by project reads the namespace list, and an unreadable list is an error). If you cannot read part of the data, the command still exits 0: each section it could not read in full is named in data.degraded ({section, state, code, target}), and each entry has one warning. The command fails when any of these required reads fails: finding the cluster by id or name and listing the pods always; finding the project by id or name and listing the project's namespaces with --project; listing the namespaces with --by project, and listing the projects with --by project and no --project; listing the nodes with --by node, or reading the named node with --by node --node N. Section that can degrade: metrics (unavailable - the CPU and memory usage figures are left out; the request and limit totals are still shown). With --project, if the project has no namespaces, the command reads no pods or metrics: the result has no rows (with --by project --project X, a single row with zero requests and limits).

create.note: Rancher takes an etcd snapshot on every etcd node of the cluster, then restarts the Kubernetes server on each etcd node, one node at a time; each snapshot appears as an etcd-snapshot object in the cluster's namespace once Rancher reads it from the cluster

Rancher stops Kubernetes on every node of the cluster (its API server is down until the restore ends), removes the server certificate and credential directories (server/tls, server/cred) on the etcd and control plane nodes, replaces the cluster's etcd data with the snapshot in spec.args.name, then starts the nodes again one at a time: every Kubernetes object created or changed after the snapshot was taken is lost, objects deleted since then come back, workloads run again from the restored objects, and Rancher deletes the Node objects of nodes that are no longer part of the cluster; deleting this object does not undo the restore, and a restore that fails can leave the cluster stopped

Rancher creates a new secrets encryption key for the cluster and re-encrypts every Secret with it, then restarts the Kubernetes server on each etcd and control plane node, one node at a time; deleting this object does not undo the rotation, and Rancher asks for an etcd restore when a rotation fails: changes made after the newest etcd snapshot cannot be restored then
Rancher issues new certificates for the services in spec.args.services, every service when it is empty, and restarts those services one node at a time; deleting this object does not undo the rotation
